title: Former Tropical Storm Edouard lingers over Texas, flooding homes and roads
text:
LIVINGSTON, Texas — Texas authorities rescued dozens of people from stranded cars, homes surrounded by floodwaters and an assisted living facility Wednesday as former Tropical Storm Edouard lingered over rural parts of the state and dumped nearly 2 feet of rain in some places.
Heavy rains from the storm, which weakened into a tropical depression after making landfall Tuesday, were expected to threaten the eastern part of the state through Thursday morning, the National Weather Service said.
Meanwhile, a burst of tropical weather persisted in the Pacific Ocean, where three hurricanes were churning in open waters.
In Texas’ hard-hit Hardin County, about 85 miles northeast of Houston, flooding, downed trees and power lines, debris, and power outages were still creating hazardous conditions, officials said.
Between 18 inches and 20 inches fell in parts of the county over the last two days, the weather service said. The average local monthly rainfall for September is just 5.51 inches, said Nick Slaughter, a meteorologist with the weather service.
Across the area close to the Louisiana border, schools and municipal offices were closed, and residents were told to stay home.
Edouard downs trees, floods roads and leaves drivers stranded
Hardin County’s office of emergency management said Wednesday afternoon that 12 motorists had to be rescued after driving into flooded roadways, two people had to be rescued from a flooded home, about 10 structures were damaged by trees and thousands were still without power.
In Jefferson County, located about 80 miles northeast of Houston, the main concern was restoring power after trees and limbs were brought down during the storm, which had wind gusts up to 90 mph, said Robert Grimm, the county emergency management coordinator. About 22,000 customers in the county were without power as of late Wednesday afternoon, nearly half of the 50,000 utility customers affected statewide, according to poweroutage.com.
Grady Leger said that as the storm moved through Hardin County on Tuesday evening, a power line went down by his home near Lumberton, and he could feel the vibration coming up from the ground.
“Some blue and yellow, white sparks caught part of my dead tree on fire,” Leger said.
An assisted living facility was damaged in Hardin County, and 21 people were evacuated, according to Texas Parks and Wildlife, whose game wardens assisted. Photos from the agency showed some officials wading in thigh-deep water in parts of the county.
Edouard is expected to dissipate Thursday.
3 hurricanes are in the Pacific Ocean
Hurricane Marie strengthened from a tropical storm on Wednesday well offshore of southwest Mexico in the Pacific, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said.
Swells generated by the storm were expected to affect parts of coastal southwestern Mexico and the Baja California peninsula over the next few days. They will likely spread to Southern California over the weekend, the center said.
Hurricane Lowell, a Category 4 storm, was hundreds of miles south of Hawaii on Wednesday. It briefly strengthened to a Category 5 storm before weakening again, and it was expected to remain powerful over the next several days. Swells generated by Lowell are likely to affect parts of the Hawaiian Islands beginning Wednesday, the center said.
Regarding Marie and Lowell, swells “are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the center said.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Karina strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm. Forecasters said it should weaken over the next few days.

images.caption: Flooding near Honey Island, Texas, after Tropical Storm Edouard, on Wednesday. Brett Coomer / Houston Chronicle via AP
Satellite imagery captured Wednesday shows three storms in the Pacific Ocean: from left, Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie. CIRA / NOAA via AP

title: Rep. David Schweikert describes surviving deadly Grand Canyon flash flood
text:
Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
Schweikert told NBC News from his office in Washington on Tuesday that the loud crash was followed by a powerful stream of mud and debris-filled water.
Two visitors died and another is still missing after flash flooding from a sudden deluge of rain briefly transformed Bright Angel Creek into a full-fledged river. About 80 people were evacuated from campsites around the historic Phantom Ranch area of the park.
The retiring member of Congress and the rest of his group were about 100 yards away from the danger zone without cellphone service. His guide led the group to an area off the Colorado River near Bright Angel Creek.
They later left the area on foot — traveling on higher ground — and camped for the night nearby.
It is “monsoon season” in Arizona, but Schweikert said there was not more than a drizzle of precipitation where he was when the dangerous flood ripped through, underscoring the potential randomness of such events.
“At some point, you realized this is a big deal; something’s really gone haywire. ... It was a ginormous flash flood,” he said.
The intricate terrain of the Grand Canyon can invite the type of deadly flood conditions that hit the southern part of the national park over the weekend.
“The deluge downpour could have been miles away and was channeled into the canyon, and what used to be a creek now is a river,” said Schweikert, who is a regular Grand Canyon hiker.
The water supply system for the park was also severely damaged, along with part of a new $208 million water pipeline project that was underway near the ranch.
Schweikert said he would likely be involved in working to get the damage addressed once proper assessments are made. “Right now, the heartbreak is a couple of people lost their lives,” he added.
He also cautioned visitors to the park to carefully monitor the weather and to use extreme caution if storms are expected in the vicinity at all. If storms are nearby, hikes through narrow passages known as slot canyons should be strictly avoided because of the risk of getting trapped, the seasoned adventurer said.
“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said.

images.caption: “It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Rep. David Schweikert said. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

videos.caption: Crews at the Grand Canyon are confronting difficult terrain as they try to find a missing hiker. We’re also seeing new images of flash flooding in Zion National Park. NBC News’ Dana Griffin is in the flood zone.

title: Months before fatal Grand Canyon flood, park service warned of elevated risk
text:
Months before a deadly flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon on Saturday, the National Park Service warned that a giant wildfire had left parts of the North Rim more vulnerable to sudden, destructive rushes of water.

title: At least 1 dead, more than a dozen missing at Grand Canyon after extreme flash flooding
text:
At least one person is dead and more than a dozen others are missing or unaccounted for, park officials said, after flash floods overwhelmed a remote area of the Grand Canyon Sunday.
Forecasters warned that more flash flooding was possible on Monday. The biggest threat of flash flooding on Monday is set to be just north of the Grand Canyon.
The catastrophic flooding prompted the National Park Service to cancel or bar all overnight stays, and impose water conservation measures.
The National Park Service is asking for information about anyone who may have been hiking or backpacking along Bright Angel Creek in Arizona, as well as campers with plans to stay at Phantom Ranch or the Bright Angel Campground.
Officials are also trying to track down travelers who might have been stranded along the North Kaibab Trail.
The National Park Service said in an evening update that a 46-year-old man was recovered from Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. The Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office was at the scene, the NPS said.
The flooding is already restricting the visitors’ use of the canyon.
All park concessions will halt overnight accommodations during the peak visitor season and water restrictions on the South Rim will begin as of noon on Monday, the NPS said. There had been “extensive damage” to infrastructure in the inner canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, which supplies water from the canyon for use in the park, it said.
“The waterline is currently not operational, leaving the park with limited water reserves and requiring significant water conservation measures to ensure available supplies can be maintained,” the service said.
The National Weather Service warned that the threat of flash flooding in all of northern and central Arizona remained through Monday evening.
The park service earlier Sunday said 15 people were missing or unaccounted for, down from a previous estimate of 20.
Among those missing is a Texas chiropractor who had been chronicling his trip to the Grand Canyon on Facebook. His sister told the New York Times that they last spoke to him on Saturday afternoon before the flooding began.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail. Additional evacuations from Phantom Ranch and the Cottonwood Campground were expected.
Park administrators also said that footbridges along Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, “eliminating hiker access across the creek,” and that certain Colorado River crossings were closed while damage is assessed.
“The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon,” the National Park Service said in a statement. “Grand Canyon National Park staff are continuing to assess damage to trails, bridges, utilities, facilities and other infrastructure.”
Phantom Ranch is accessible only by hiking, raft or mule transport. It has been a coveted Grand Canyon destination since it opened in 1922.
Colorado River traffic was also shut down because of the risk of floating debris.
David Gregory was one of many in the area on Sunday. He told NBC News he spent Saturday morning hiking down the North Kaibab Trail to Phantom Ranch and had just checked into a cabin a couple of hours before the rain hit.
Hours later, officials told him and his group they needed to evacuate. After grabbing their things, Gregory said they crossed some footbridges before first responders airlifted him and about 50 others to safety.
“It was kind of crazy hearing later that the bridge that we crossed was wiped out. Kind of makes you think that maybe we should have been in more of a panic,” Gregory said.

images.caption: Heavy flooding in Grand Canyon National Park on Sunday. Craig Sanderson via AP
Remnants of stone bridge pylons remain along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood that destroyed the footbridge Saturday. Grand Canyon National Park
